sentence: The NHS lists sitting or standing for long periods, a high-salt diet, being overweight, pregnancy and some medicines among the more common causes of swollen ankles and legs.
Less often, swelling comes from a blood clot, an infection, or a heart, kidney or liver problem.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs does not improve after a few days of home care, gets worse, or occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.
Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood or feeling faint with leg swelling may mean a clot in the lungs, which needs a 999 call.
note: NHS page and NHS 111 Wales page as summarised

sentence: The NHS calls swollen ankles, feet and legs oedema, which is a build-up of fluid in the body’s tissues.
note: Page title is oedema; the plain definition is a textbook gloss

sentence: The NHS lists sitting or standing still for long periods, a high-salt diet and being overweight as lifestyle factors.
Pregnancy, varicose veins and thyroid problems can also cause swelling.
Some medicines are listed too, including certain blood pressure medicines, contraceptive pills, hormone therapy, antidepressants and steroids.
Less commonly, swelling can follow an injury or an insect bite, or come from a blood clot or an infection.
The NHS also lists problems with the heart, kidneys or liver as causes.
The British Heart Foundation adds lymphoedema, a problem with the drainage of lymph fluid, as another cause.
NHS 111 Wales advises seeking advice for swelling in only one leg when there is no known cause.
The NHS describes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) as throbbing pain in one leg, usually in the calf or thigh, with swelling in that leg.
The skin over a DVT can look red, blue or darker than usual.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs has not improved after a few days of home care, if it gets worse, or if it occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.
NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for swelling that is severe, painful, sudden, red or hot, or that comes with a high temperature or shivering.
The same page lists swelling in the feet, ankles or legs of a person with diabetes as a reason for urgent advice.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if leg swelling comes with shortness of breath or chest pain, because a clot can travel to the lungs.
note: NHS DVT and oedema pages as summarised

sentence: Coughing up blood or feeling faint are also described as symptoms of a clot in the lungs.
In pregnancy, very severe swelling of the hands, face or ankles with nausea can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, and NHS inform says to contact a midwife or GP straight away.
note: NHS inform pregnancy page as summarised

sentence: The NHS says swelling in the ankles, feet or legs often goes away on its own.
note: Search summary of NHS oedema page

sentence: Its self-care advice includes raising the swollen area on a chair or pillows, gentle exercise such as walking, and avoiding long periods of standing or sitting.
note: Search summary of NHS oedema page

sentence: Wide, comfortable shoes with a low heel and washing and moisturising the feet to prevent infection are also mentioned.
note: Search summary of NHS oedema page

sentence: Treatment for swelling that does not settle depends on the cause, and lifestyle changes such as losing weight or eating less salt may help.
note: Search summary of NHS oedema page

sentence: The British Heart Foundation says heart failure is treated with medicines that help the heart pump better and diuretics, which help remove fluid from the tissues.
note: Search summary attributing this to BHF
